source.title: Cluster-based pruning techniques for audio data
source.authors: Boris Bergsma; M. Brzezińska; O. Yazyev; Milos Cernak

record.tranche_reason: The study measures loss scaling in audio classification and reports that scaling may break down or cross over between regimes; it also finds fitted exponents vary with model size and pruning strategy. This is a refinement in an audio setting, not a reproduction of language-model scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The study tests loss against training-set size for audio keyword-spotting classifiers, not language-model pretraining loss against parameters, tokens, or compute. Rows record the reported loss-scaling exponents and the stated possible breakdown or crossover. Scaling claims cited from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The study is mainly about data pruning, but it fits loss against training-set size for audio keyword-spotting CNNs. That gives a weak test of power-law form in a new modality (V5) and of how exponents shift with data selection and bend at larger N (V7). It is a new setting rather than a refutation, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present k-means cluster-based audio data pruning as a proof of principle. Simple pruning generally gives slightly larger loss-scaling exponents and better accuracy at large N, while hard pruning lowers exponents. They note the exponent differences are not pronounced and scaling may break down or cross over at larger N. Transfer of the scaling results to other datasets remains open.
record.recipe_differences: Uses supervised audio keyword-spotting classifiers and loss versus training-set size, with data pruning; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining scaling measurements.
record.method_sensitivity: Reported exponents vary with network size and pruning method/fraction. The authors state that some increasing-N points may reflect breakdowns or crossovers and were excluded from exponent calculations.

fits_no_version.finding: The tiny 3.5k-parameter model has a much smaller data-scaling exponent (0.244) than the 29k and 270k models (0.396 and 0.391), which are similar to each other.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The data-scaling exponent drops when model capacity is the bottleneck and saturates once the model is large enough.

record.problems: The experiments use one audio dataset and three small CNNs. Some points were excluded from exponent calculations because scaling might break down or cross over; the authors say the tiny-model exponent has greater uncertainty. Transfer to other datasets is not established.

untested.parts: Scaling with model parameters or compute in audio; image or video models; repeated data; fine-tuning and transfer. Only loss vs training-set size, on one small dataset with three tiny CNNs.
Parameter-counting conventions, training schedule, fitting-method comparisons and compute-optimal splits. Only the data-selection (pruning) effect on the exponent and curve bending are touched.
Not tested; the 'extrapolation' in Fig. 2 is illustrative, not a validated prediction.
Accuracy is reported vs N, but not as a scaling prediction from loss.

missing.what: Range of N and number of points used in each fit; which points were excluded; goodness of fit
Q-score pruning baseline reported to perform like random pruning (no exponent given)

record.verdict_notes: This is a data-pruning paper that uses the scaling exponent as a metric, so it sits near T4. It is kept as T3 only because it reports exponents for unpruned-baseline (random) data and an observed breakdown or crossover. Rows R02-R27 compare the study's own method with the random baseline; they bear only on V7 (data dependence), not V5. The models are tiny CNNs on one dataset, so the evidential weight is low.

versions.untested_parts: The study is not about language models and does not test held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
It does not test whether fits from small runs predict much larger runs.
It does not vary parameter and token allocations at fixed compute or estimate compute-optimal allocations.
It does not compare architectures at fixed parameter count to test the effect of depth, width, or other architecture details.
Tests loss scaling with training-set size in one audio keyword-spotting dataset and pruning setup; it does not test image or video models, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
It reports classification accuracy, but does not test downstream-task performance as a function of model scale or pretraining loss.

It tests variation with model size, pruning strategy, and fitting range in audio loss-versus-sample-size curves. It does not test parameter-counting conventions, language-model training schedules or data, or compute-optimal splits.

rows.subject: tiny, small, and large KWS NNs (aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Assess loss-scaling curves as training-set size N increases; some points were excluded from exponent fitting.

conditions.value: Google Speech Commands Dataset V3 KWS
log-log fits; points excluded where scaling might break down or cross over

rows.measure: Whether a single power-law scaling behavior describes loss across increasing N
rows.value: The authors report that increasing N may show either a breakdown of power-law scaling or a crossover between regimes with different exponents; they excluded such points from exponent calculations.
rows.note: The authors also state that loss scaling with dataset size or model parameters may be more complicated and not necessarily monotonic.
rows.check: A qualitative statement only: the curves may break down or cross over at larger N. No numbers are given, and the affected points were dropped from the fits.

source_check.correct: V5: partial; V7: observed, qualitatively. Possible breakdown or crossover qualifies a single power law while supporting V7's allowance for bending curves.
source_check.problem: One partial state does not fit both linked versions: the reported departure from a single power law supports V7.

relationships.condition: Random-pruning loss vs training-set size for 3.5k, 29k and 270k-parameter audio KWS CNNs, over the included N range
relationships.reason: Log-log fits yield exponents 0.244, 0.396 and 0.391 with small stated errors (R01, R10, R19). Fit quality and N range are not reported, so this support is weak.
relationships.display_finding: Log-log fits yielded exponents of 0.244, 0.396, and 0.391 for the 3.5k-, 29k-, and 270k-parameter models, respectively, with small stated errors.

source_check.reason: Section 4.2 and Table 2 report power-law fits with exponents 0.244, 0.396 and 0.391; support is limited to the retained fitting range.

relationships.condition: Small and large CNNs with ≥20% simple pruning, or ≥20% hard pruning on the small CNN
relationships.reason: Data selection shifts exponents beyond the stated ±0.005 error, e.g. 0.396→0.413 and 0.391→0.421 (R12-R14, R16-R18, R25-R27). The authors call the differences not pronounced.
relationships.display_finding: With simple pruning of at least 20% in small and large CNNs, or hard pruning of at least 20% in the small CNN, example exponents shift from 0.396 to 0.413 and from 0.391 to 0.421, exceeding the stated ±0.005 error despite the authors describing the differences as modest.

relationships.reason: The curves may bend away from a single power law through breakdown or crossover (R28). This is stated qualitatively.
relationships.display_finding: Across all three models, increasing N may produce breakdowns or crossovers that depart from a single power law.

relationships.display_finding: Exponents matched random pruning within stated error for tiny CNNs with 10–40% hard or 10–30% simple pruning and large CNNs with hard or 10% simple pruning, but tiny-CNN 40% simple pruning gave 0.260 versus 0.244 for random pruning, exceeding the stated 0.01 error.
